problem.title: Design a Multi-Tier Semantic & Prompt Caching Layer for 100K QPS LLMs

spark.summary: Architect a 100K QPS multi-tier LLM caching platform combining L1 exact hash, L2 HNSW semantic cache with cross-encoder verification, and L3 prefix-aware RadixAttention KV routing.
spark.keyTakeaway: Serve L1/L2 hits in < 15 ms with zero GPU FLOPs, route misses via bounded-load prefix consistent hashing for 85%+ L3 KV reuse, and isolate tenants via RBAC namespace filters.
spark.byteSummary:
At 100,000 QPS, sending every LLM prompt straight to GPU inference burns millions in H100/B200 compute and blows past interactive latency SLOs. A production caching tier must serve repeated or paraphrased intents in < 15 ms while accelerating novel queries via prefix KV reuse.

The architecture places a Tenant/RBAC Namespace Filter at the API Gateway, feeding an L1 Redis/Valkey exact-hash tier (< 1 ms) and an L2 HNSW semantic cache (~7 ms) guarded by a numeric/entity parity check and cross-encoder false-positive gate (~5 ms).

Cache misses pass through a Prefix-Aware Consistent Hash Router (bounded at 1.25x average load) to vLLM/SGLang workers holding warm RadixAttention KV-block pools in HBM and offloaded DRAM. Completed non-PII responses write back asynchronously with `(model_epoch, kb_version, ttl_sec)` tags for instant O(1) invalidation.

learningJourney.title: Stage 1: 100K QPS Traffic Profile & Hit-Rate Economics
learningJourney.purpose: Quantify GPU savings, latency budgets (< 15 ms hit, < 180 ms miss TTFT), and hit-rate targets across L1, L2, and L3.
learningJourney.explanation: Assume 100K QPS with 15% exact repeats (L1), 25% semantic paraphrases (L2), and 60% novel queries sharing 4K-token system/RAG prefixes (L3). Offloading 40% of total traffic at L1/L2 cuts GPU fleet size by 40%, while L3 prefix KV reuse cuts prefill FLOPs on the remaining 60% by 80%.

sectionDiagram.title: 40% Total LLM Bypass (L1+L2) + 80% Prefill Savings (L3)

cards.label: 40K QPS GPU Offload
cards.detail: Serving 40% of queries from L1/L2 saves dozens of GPU inference pods at peak.

cards.label: 15 ms Hit SLO
cards.detail: L1 (< 1 ms) + L2 (4 ms embed + 3 ms HNSW + 5 ms cross-encoder) stays safely under 15 ms.

sectionDiagram.summary: L1 and L2 absorb 40% of 100K QPS in < 15 ms while L3 prefix KV reuse accelerates the remaining 60% on GPUs.
sectionDiagram.caption: 100K QPS splits across L1 exact (15%), L2 semantic (25%), and L3 prefix-cached GPU inference (60%).

learningJourney.title: Stage 2: Capacity Sizing for Redis/Valkey L1/L2 & KV Pools
learningJourney.purpose: Size DRAM for 100M cached prompt-response pairs, 384-D HNSW graphs, and offloaded DRAM KV blocks.
learningJourney.explanation: Storing 100M cached entries (average 2 KB response + 384-D SQ8 vector = 2.4 KB/entry) requires ~240 GB data + ~45 GB HNSW graph overhead = ~285 GB RAM (easily sharded across a 16-node Redis/Valkey cluster with 32 GB/node + RF=2). Meanwhile, each GPU host allocates 256 GB host DRAM as an L3 KV offload tier.

sectionDiagram.title: 285 GB Sharded L1/L2 Cache + Per-Node DRAM KV Offload

cards.label: Tenant-Keyed Sharding
cards.detail: Sharding L2 HNSW by tenant_id keeps every lookup to a single Redis shard (zero scatter-gather across 16 nodes).

cards.label: SQ8 Vector Savings
cards.detail: Quantizing 384-D FP32 vectors to SQ8 cuts vector RAM 4x from 153 GB to 38.4 GB.

sectionDiagram.summary: Sharding 100M SQ8 HNSW entries by tenant_id fits in a 16-node Redis/Valkey cluster with single-shard lookup latency.
sectionDiagram.caption: 100M responses and 384-D SQ8 HNSW vectors shard across 16 Redis/Valkey nodes by tenant_id.

learningJourney.title: Stage 3: Tenant/RBAC Namespace Filtering & Security
learningJourney.purpose: Guarantee zero cross-tenant or cross-permission cache leaks in multi-tenant RAG deployments.
learningJourney.explanation: In enterprise RAG, two users in the same org may have different document ACLs. The API Gateway computes an `rbac_scope_hash` from the caller's `tenant_id` and role/ACL group IDs and enforces it as a mandatory pre-filter on L1 keys, L2 HNSW searches, and L3 KV prefix sharing—preventing unauthorized context leakage.

sectionDiagram.title: Mandatory RBAC Namespace Scoping Across L1, L2 & L3

cards.label: Zero Cross-ACL Hits
cards.detail: Users with different ACL groups never share L1/L2 RAG responses or private document KV prefixes.

cards.label: Shared Public Base
cards.detail: Global non-sensitive system instructions can still share a common public prefix namespace.

sectionDiagram.summary: Deriving an rbac_scope_hash at the gateway enforces strict tenant and ACL isolation across every cache tier.
sectionDiagram.caption: Gateway-computed rbac_scope_hash isolates L1, L2, and L3 caches per tenant and ACL group.

learningJourney.title: Stage 4: Embedding + HNSW + Cross-Encoder Pipeline
learningJourney.purpose: Execute the 12 ms L2 semantic lookup pipeline with bounded tail latency and circuit-breaker bypass.
learningJourney.explanation: At 100K QPS, an ONNX Runtime pool (Triton/ORT) batches incoming misses every 1 ms to embed queries in ~4 ms, queries the tenant's Redis/Valkey HNSW shard (~3 ms), and runs a quantized INT8 TinyBERT cross-encoder on Top-1 matches (~5 ms). If L2 latency exceeds 20 ms, a circuit breaker bypasses L2 straight to L3 GPU inference.

sectionDiagram.title: 12 ms L2 Semantic Pipeline with 20 ms Circuit Breaker

cards.label: INT8 Cross-Encoder
cards.detail: Quantizing the cross-encoder to INT8 cuts pair-verification latency to ~5 ms on CPU/L4 GPUs.

cards.label: Fail-Open Bypass
cards.detail: Caches are pure accelerators; if Redis or ONNX degrades, traffic fails open cleanly to GPU inference.

sectionDiagram.summary: Micro-batched ONNX embeddings, single-shard HNSW, INT8 cross-encoder gating, and a 20 ms circuit breaker keep L2 fast and safe.
sectionDiagram.caption: ONNX embedding, single-shard HNSW, and INT8 cross-encoder run in ~12 ms behind a 20 ms fail-open circuit breaker.

learningJourney.title: Stage 5: Bounded-Load Prefix Consistent Hash Router
learningJourney.purpose: Route 60K QPS of cache misses to warm vLLM/SGLang RadixAttention workers without hot-spotting.
learningJourney.explanation: The miss router hashes the first 512 tokens of the prompt onto a consistent hash ring with virtual nodes (150 vnodes/GPU replica) to maximize L3 KV prefix hits. To protect against viral tenant prompts, if the primary replica's active KV/queue load exceeds 1.25x cluster average, the router walks clockwise to the next replica.

sectionDiagram.title: Consistent Hash Ring + 1.25x Bounded-Load Spillover

cards.label: Graceful Autoscaling
cards.detail: Consistent hashing minimizes KV cache thrashing when GPU replicas scale up or down.

cards.label: Dual-Warm Replicas
cards.detail: High-traffic prefixes naturally warm 2-3 adjacent ring replicas during peak bursts.

sectionDiagram.summary: Virtual-node consistent hashing with 1.25x bounded-load spillover preserves L3 KV locality while preventing GPU hot spots.
sectionDiagram.caption: 512-token prefix hashing with 1.25x bounded-load spillover routes misses to warm vLLM/SGLang workers.

learningJourney.title: Stage 6: HBM-to-DRAM KV Offloading & Async Write-Back
learningJourney.purpose: Expand L3 KV prefix retention 10x via DRAM offloading and keep L1/L2 write-back off the critical path.
learningJourney.explanation: GPU HBM is scarce (80-192 GB), so active conversations can evict shared RAG KV blocks prematurely. Offloading evicted RadixAttention blocks asynchronously to 256 GB host DRAM (and restoring via pinned PCIe DMA in ~2 ms) keeps prefix hit rates high, while completed responses publish to Kafka for async L1/L2 indexing.

sectionDiagram.title: Pinned PCIe KV Offload & Asynchronous L1/L2 Write-Back

cards.label: 2 ms DMA vs 150 ms Prefill
cards.detail: Restoring 64 MB of KV blocks over PCIe Gen5 takes ~2 ms—75x faster than recomputing prefill.

cards.label: Zero User Latency
cards.detail: Async Kafka write-back decouples HNSW insertion from the user's streaming response.

sectionDiagram.summary: DRAM KV offloading restores cold prefix blocks in ~2 ms over PCIe, while Kafka async write-back keeps L1/L2 updates zero-latency.
sectionDiagram.caption: Cold KV blocks offload to 256 GB host DRAM for ~2 ms PCIe restore, while completed answers write back via Kafka.

learningJourney.title: Stage 7: Epoch Invalidation, Canary Thresholds & Observability
learningJourney.purpose: Prevent stale answers on model/KB updates and tune cosine/cross-encoder thresholds safely in production.
learningJourney.explanation: Attach `(model_epoch, kb_version, ttl_sec)` to every cache key/metadata record so rolling a new model or re-indexing RAG documents invalidates stale entries in O(1). Track `l1_hit_rate`, `l2_hit_rate`, `l2_false_positive_audit_rate`, and `l3_prefix_reuse_pct`, running shadow evaluations on 1% of L2 hits against the live LLM.

sectionDiagram.title: O(1) Epoch Invalidation & 1% Shadow False-Positive Auditing

nodes.label: 1% Shadow LLM Audit
nodes.sub: Compare L2 hit vs live LLM

cards.label: 1% Shadow Verification
cards.detail: Asynchronously running 1% of L2 hits against the live LLM measures real false-positive rates without affecting user latency.

cards.label: Domain-Specific Thresholds
cards.detail: Medical/financial tenants use stricter thresholds (CE >= 0.95) than FAQ support bots (CE >= 0.88).

sectionDiagram.summary: Epoch invalidation, 1% shadow LLM auditing, and per-domain threshold tuning keep semantic caches accurate over time.
sectionDiagram.caption: Epoch tags, 1% shadow LLM auditing, and telemetry drive safe per-domain semantic threshold tuning.

knowledgeChecks.question: Why should L2 HNSW indexes be sharded by `tenant_id` (and pre-filtered by `rbac_scope_hash`) rather than using one global HNSW index?

options.text: To guarantee zero cross-tenant/ACL leakage and keep each lookup to a single shard without 16-way scatter-gather.
options.feedback: Correct. Tenant-keyed sharding enforces security isolation and avoids multi-shard HNSW fan-out latency.

options.text: Because HNSW cannot store more than 1,000 vectors per node.
options.feedback: Incorrect. Each HNSW shard easily holds millions of 384-D vectors.

options.text: Because Redis does not support TCP connections from API Gateways.
options.feedback: Incorrect. Gateways connect to Redis/Valkey shards directly.

options.text: To disable L3 RadixAttention prefix caching.
options.feedback: Incorrect. L2 sharding complements L3 KV prefix caching.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Sharding and filtering L2 HNSW by tenant/RBAC scope eliminates cross-tenant data leaks and avoids multi-shard scatter-gather overhead.

knowledgeChecks.question: What happens if Redis/Valkey or the ONNX embedding tier experiences a latency spike above 20 ms?

options.text: The 20 ms fail-open circuit breaker bypasses L2 and routes the request directly to L3 GPU inference.
options.feedback: Correct. Caches are pure latency/cost accelerators and should fail open to inference rather than blocking requests.

options.text: The API Gateway drops all incoming requests with HTTP 500.
options.feedback: Incorrect. Failing closed on a cache spike turns a cache issue into a full outage.

options.text: The GPU cluster flushes all HBM KV blocks.
options.feedback: Incorrect. GPU KV caches remain intact to accelerate the bypassed misses.
Incorrect. Retrying synchronously would worsen tail latency.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: A fail-open circuit breaker ensures L2 cache slowdowns degrade gracefully to GPU inference without causing outages.

knowledgeChecks.question: Why is offloading cold RadixAttention KV blocks to 256 GB host DRAM effective when GPU HBM fills up?

options.text: Restoring a 64 MB KV prefix over PCIe DMA takes ~2 ms—far faster than recomputing 4K-token prefill on the GPU.
options.feedback: Correct. Pinned PCIe DMA restoration is orders of magnitude faster than full attention prefill.

options.text: Because host DRAM runs CUDA attention kernels faster than HBM.
options.feedback: Incorrect. Attention kernels still run in GPU HBM after DMA restore.

options.text: Because DRAM KV blocks replace the L1 exact-hash cache.
options.feedback: Incorrect. DRAM KV blocks extend L3 prefix capacity, not L1 response caching.
Incorrect. RBAC scope isolation still applies to L3 prefix keys.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Host DRAM KV offloading expands prefix cache capacity 10x while restoring blocks over PCIe in ~2 ms vs ~150 ms prefill.

beginner.summary: Build a multi-layer AI cache that checks exact matches first, then similar meanings, and finally reuses shared prompt prefixes on GPUs.
beginner.keyTakeaway: Checking fast caches before calling the GPU cuts response time to ~12 ms on hits and keeps misses fast.
beginner.byteSummary:
At 100,000 requests per second, checking an exact cache and a meaning-based vector cache handles 40% of traffic without touching a GPU.

The remaining requests go to GPU servers that already have the shared system prompt cached in memory.

intermediate.summary: Combine tenant-sharded Redis L1/L2 (384-D SQ8 HNSW + INT8 cross-encoder), 20 ms fail-open circuit breakers, and bounded-load prefix consistent hashing.
intermediate.keyTakeaway: Single-shard tenant HNSW + cross-encoder gating hits < 15 ms, while 1.25x bounded-load prefix hashing preserves 85%+ L3 KV locality.
intermediate.byteSummary:
The gateway derives an `rbac_scope_hash`, probes L1 SHA-256 (< 1 ms) and L2 tenant-sharded HNSW + INT8 cross-encoder (~12 ms) behind a 20 ms fail-open breaker.

Misses route via 1.25x bounded-load consistent hashing over the first 512 tokens to warm vLLM/SGLang RadixAttention workers.

advanced.summary: Add 256 GB host DRAM KV offloading (~2 ms PCIe DMA restore), Kafka async write-back with PII/error filtering, O(1) epoch invalidation, and 1% shadow LLM audits.
advanced.keyTakeaway: PCIe DRAM KV offloading expands L3 capacity 10x, while epoch tags and 1% shadow audits maintain freshness and low false-positive rates.
advanced.byteSummary:
Offloading cold RadixAttention blocks to 256 GB host DRAM restores 64 MB prefixes in ~2 ms over PCIe (75x faster than prefill). Completed non-PII responses write back via Kafka tagged with `(model_epoch, kb_version, ttl_sec)`.

A 1% shadow audit continuously measures L2 false-positive rates against the live LLM to tune per-domain thresholds.
